\chapter{Animals}
\label{ch:te-animals}
\hlchaptermodality{60}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five common animals in Telugu, and greet the house that keeps them.}

Complete TE-C60-bird and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gēde]{\te{గేదె} (gēde) — a buffalo}

\label{lesson:TE-C60-buffalo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nippu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గేదె}}
\textbf{\te{గేదె}} (\emph{gēde}) — \textquotedblleft{}a buffalo\textquotedblright{}.

\te{గేదె} is the water buffalo — black, unhurried, and the animal most of the \te{పాలు} in a Telugu household actually come from. The cow gets the songs; the \te{గేదె} fills the pot.

The word is inherited, and the animal is so ordinary that arriving at a village house often means being met by one before anybody comes out to say \te{నమస్కారం}.

A \te{గేదె} standing in a \te{చెరువు} with only its nose above the water is the picture the word carries. That is where it spends the hottest part of the day.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first animal.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gēde}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gēde}, then \emph{pālu}, and say which one gives the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గేదె} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a buffalo\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mēka]{\te{మేక} (mēka) — a goat}

\label{lesson:TE-C60-goat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gēde} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మేక}}
\textbf{\te{మేక}} (\emph{mēka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a goat\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మేక} is the goat: small, loud, and kept by households that cannot keep a \te{గేదె}. Where the buffalo wants water and grazing, the \te{మేక} wants almost nothing and will eat what is left.

The word is inherited and it is old. Its shape sits close to the Tamil and Kannada words for the same animal, which is what happens to the names of animals people have kept for a very long time.

A \te{మేక} will strip a bush bare and move on, which is why a \te{గ్రామం} keeps them at its edge rather than in its lanes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: one for milk, one for anything.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mēka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mēka}, then \emph{gēde}, and say which one wants the \te{చెరువు}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మేక} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a goat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kōḍi]{\te{కోడి} (kōḍi) — a hen}

\label{lesson:TE-C60-hen}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mēka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కోడి}}
\textbf{\te{కోడి}} (\emph{kōḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a hen\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కోడి} is the domestic fowl, hen or cock alike; the word does not divide them, and when the difference matters a second word goes in front.

It is inherited and it is everywhere in the family, close in shape to the Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam words for the same bird — one of those words that travelled with the animal and has not moved since.

The \te{కోడి} is also the village clock. It wakes a house before \te{ఉదయం} is properly under way, which is why nobody there has ever needed a \te{గంట}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kōḍi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kōḍi}, then \emph{mēka}, and say which one wakes you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కోడి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a hen\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cīma]{\te{చీమ} (cīma) — an ant}

\label{lesson:TE-C60-ant}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kōḍi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చీమ}}
\textbf{\te{చీమ}} (\emph{cīma}) — \textquotedblleft{}an ant\textquotedblright{}.

\te{చీమ} is the ant. After a \te{గేదె} and a \te{కోడి} it is a jump in scale worth making, because the same plain word-making covers whatever lives in a house, however small it is.

The word is inherited. Telugu has a stock comparison about a \te{చీమ} carrying many times its own weight, and it is the ordinary way to praise somebody small who works hard.

A line of \te{చీమలు} across a floor usually ends at a \te{పండు} somebody left out.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: the biggest and the smallest so far.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cīma}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cīma}, then \emph{gēde}, and say which one is easier to miss
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చీమ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an ant\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pakṣi]{\te{పక్షి} (pakṣi) — a bird}

\label{lesson:TE-C60-bird}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cīma} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పక్షి}}
\textbf{\te{పక్షి}} (\emph{pakṣi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bird\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పక్షి} is the general one: any bird at all, the \te{కోడి} included. It came in from Sanskrit, and beside it Telugu keeps its own \te{పిట్ట} for the small ones about a garden.

That is a split this book has met before — an inherited word doing the everyday work and a borrowed one carrying the wider idea, the same shape as \te{నిప్పు} beside \te{అగ్ని}. Once you start expecting it, half the vocabulary sorts itself.

Five animals now, from the \te{గేదె} at the gate to the \te{చీమ} under it, and a \te{నమస్కారం} for whoever keeps them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{గేదె}, \te{మేక}, \te{కోడి}, \te{చీమ}, \te{పక్షి}. Enough to greet a house and name what lives in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pakṣi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{namaskāram} to whoever keeps them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పక్షి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bird\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
